Computing engines and control of VLMC with covariates

Source: vignettes/articles/covlmc-engines.Rmd
covlmc-engines.Rmd
library(mixvlmc)

A VLMC with covariates (COVLMC, see vignette("covlmc")) associates a logistic model to each of its contexts. Those models are fitted by external packages, called computing engines in mixvlmc. This article describes the available engines, their differences and the parameters that control the estimation of the logistic models. It also explains how to reduce the memory occupied by COVLMC objects, which store the fitted models.

Computing engines

Choosing an engine

The engine is selected with the mixvlmc.predictive option (see ?mixvlmc-package for the list of the package options). Two values are supported:

  • "glm" (default value): covlmc() uses stats::glm() with the binomial family when the time series has two states, and VGAM::vglm() with the multinomial family when it has three states or more;
  • "multinom": covlmc() uses nnet::multinom() in all cases.

The engine can be changed for the rest of the session with options():

old_options <- options(mixvlmc.predictive = "multinom")
## covlmc() and tune_covlmc() use now nnet::multinom()
options(old_options) ## back to the previous engine

To use an engine only for some computations, it is simpler to rely on withr::with_options() (or on withr::local_options() inside a function), as done in the rest of this article.

The engine used by covlmc() is recorded in the model. When prune() fits new models for a COVLMC (tune_covlmc() relies on prune()), it uses the recorded engine, with a warning if the option has been changed in between.

A running example

We use the household electricity consumption data set (powerconsumption, see also vignette("covlmc")), restricted to its fifth week and discretised in three states. The covariate indicates whether the measurement was made during the day.

pc_week_5 <- powerconsumption[powerconsumption$week == 5, ]
elec_dts <- cut(pc_week_5$active_power,
  breaks = c(0, 0.4, 2, 8),
  labels = c("low", "typical", "high")
)
elec_cov <- data.frame(day = pc_week_5$hour >= 7 & pc_week_5$hour <= 17)

We select a model with the AIC with the default engine (here VGAM::vglm() as the time series has three states):

elec_glm <- tune_covlmc(elec_dts, elec_cov, criterion = "AIC")
elec_glm
#> VLMC with covariates context tree on low, typical, high 
#>  cutoff in quantile scale: 0.1715
#>  Number of contexts: 5 
#>  Maximum context length: 2 
#>  Selected by AIC (1000.052) with likelihood function "truncated" (-487.0262)

and with nnet::multinom():

elec_multinom <- withr::with_options(
  list(mixvlmc.predictive = "multinom"),
  tune_covlmc(elec_dts, elec_cov, criterion = "AIC")
)
elec_multinom
#> VLMC with covariates context tree on low, typical, high 
#>  cutoff in quantile scale: 0.1715
#>  Number of contexts: 5 
#>  Maximum context length: 2 
#>  Selected by AIC (1000.053) with likelihood function "truncated" (-487.0264)

The two engines lead to the same context tree, with very close likelihoods and AIC. The models are shown below with their coefficients, first for VGAM::vglm():

model_glm <- as_covlmc(elec_glm)
draw(model_glm, model = "full")
#> ▪
#> ├─ low ([ (I)    • day_1TRUE
#> │         -1.558 • 1.006     ])
#> ├─ typical
#> │  ├─ low ([ (I)   
#> │  │         0.3365
#> │  │         -1.609 ])
#> │  ├─ typical ([ (I)   
#> │  │             2.937 
#> │  │             0.3747 ])
#> │  └─ high ([ (I)  
#> │             2.773
#> │             1.705 ])
#> └─ high ([ (I)   • day_1TRUE
#>            17.41 • -14.23   
#>            19.38 • -14.88    ])

and then for nnet::multinom():

model_multinom <- as_covlmc(elec_multinom)
draw(model_multinom, model = "full")
#> ▪
#> ├─ low ([ (I)    • day_1TRUE
#> │         -1.558 • 1.006     ])
#> ├─ typical
#> │  ├─ low ([ (I)   
#> │  │         0.3365
#> │  │         -1.609 ])
#> │  ├─ typical ([ (I)   
#> │  │             2.937 
#> │  │             0.3747 ])
#> │  └─ high ([ (I)  
#> │             2.773
#> │             1.705 ])
#> └─ high ([ (I)   • day_1TRUE
#>            11.56 • -8.385   
#>            13.53 • -9.029    ])

Most of the coefficients are identical (up to the displayed precision), but the ones of the high context are very different.

Estimation algorithms and separable data

The engines maximise the same likelihood, but with different algorithms: stats::glm() and VGAM::vglm() use iteratively reweighted least squares, while nnet::multinom() uses a quasi-Newton optimisation method (BFGS). When the maximum likelihood estimator exists, the algorithms reach it (up to numerical precision) and the coefficients agree, as in most of the contexts above.

This is not the case when the data of a context are (almost) separable, for instance when a value of a covariate determines the next state. Let us look at the states that follow the high state, depending on the value of the covariate:

elec_states <- as.character(elec_dts)
after_high <- which(head(elec_states, -1) == "high")
high_table <- table(
  day = elec_cov$day[after_high],
  next_state = elec_states[after_high + 1]
)
high_table
#>        next_state
#> day     high low typical
#>   FALSE  150   0      21
#>   TRUE    90   1      24

The high state is never followed by the low one at night and very rarely during the day (in 1 of the 115 transitions from high). With low as the reference state, the logistic model of the high context describes the logarithm of the ratio between the probability of typical (respectively high) and the one of low as the sum of an intercept and of a coefficient for day_1TRUE, the value of the covariate at the time of the last high state. As the probability of low at night is zero in the data, the maximum likelihood intercepts are infinite (and the coefficients of day_1TRUE are minus infinity, as low has a non-zero probability during the day).

The algorithms therefore make the intercepts grow until their stopping criterion is met: as the likelihood barely changes once the probability of low at night is small enough, the algorithms stop at different (large) values. We can compare the probabilities estimated by the two models of the high context:

high_probs <- function(fitted) {
  coefs <- unname(as.matrix(model(find_sequence(fitted, "high"))))
  ## logits with respect to the reference state (low)
  eta <- rbind(night = c(0, coefs[, 1]), day = c(0, coefs[, 1] + coefs[, 2]))
  probs <- exp(eta) / rowSums(exp(eta))
  colnames(probs) <- states(fitted)
  probs
}
high_probs(model_glm)
#>                low   typical      high
#> night 3.366147e-09 0.1228070 0.8771930
#> day   8.695652e-03 0.2086957 0.7826087
high_probs(model_multinom)
#>                low   typical      high
#> night 1.168289e-06 0.1228000 0.8771989
#> day   8.695001e-03 0.2086925 0.7826125

The probabilities agree except for the probability of low at night, which is tiny in both cases but differs by several orders of magnitude. This has almost no effect on the likelihood:

logLik(model_glm)
#> 'log Lik.' -487.0262 (df=13)
logLik(model_multinom)
#> 'log Lik.' -487.0264 (df=13)

In general, such differences have no practical consequences. However the coefficients of separable contexts should not be interpreted (only their signs are meaningful), and as covlmc() relies on likelihood ratio tests to simplify the models, a test whose p-value is close to the cut off alpha can lead to different decisions with the two engines, and thus to different models.

Convergence and the mixvlmc.maxit option

The maximal number of iterations of the engines is given by the mixvlmc.maxit option (100 by default). When it is reached, stats::glm() and VGAM::vglm() report a warning (a message is reported instead when this concerns a model that is discarded because it is rank deficient), while nnet::multinom() does not.

We illustrate this with a binary version of the electricity consumption time series, for which the "glm" engine uses stats::glm(). The following function counts the warnings emitted by an expression rather than displaying them:

count_warnings <- function(expr) {
  nb_warnings <- 0
  value <- withCallingHandlers(expr, warning = function(w) {
    nb_warnings <<- nb_warnings + 1
    invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
  })
  list(value = value, warnings = nb_warnings)
}
elec_bin <- cut(pc_week_5$active_power,
  breaks = c(0, 2, 8),
  labels = c("normal", "high")
)
bin_glm <- covlmc(elec_bin, elec_cov, alpha = 0.1)
bin_glm_5 <- withr::with_options(
  list(mixvlmc.maxit = 5),
  count_warnings(covlmc(elec_bin, elec_cov, alpha = 0.1))
)
bin_glm_5$warnings
#> [1] 8

With at most 5 iterations, stats::glm() reports 8 convergence warnings, but the resulting model has the same likelihood as the one obtained with the default number of iterations:

logLik(bin_glm)
#> 'log Lik.' -283.846 (df=5)
logLik(bin_glm_5$value)
#> 'log Lik.' -283.846 (df=5)

Indeed most of the warnings concern models fitted on (almost) separable data, for which there is no finite solution to converge to: stopping the iterations earlier has almost no effect on their likelihood. The situation is different with nnet::multinom():

bin_multinom <- withr::with_options(
  list(mixvlmc.predictive = "multinom"),
  covlmc(elec_bin, elec_cov, alpha = 0.1)
)
bin_multinom_5 <- withr::with_options(
  list(mixvlmc.predictive = "multinom", mixvlmc.maxit = 5),
  count_warnings(covlmc(elec_bin, elec_cov, alpha = 0.1))
)
bin_multinom_5$warnings
#> [1] 0

No warning is reported, but the model obtained with at most 5 iterations is not the one obtained with the default value:

logLik(bin_multinom)
#> 'log Lik.' -283.846 (df=5)
logLik(bin_multinom_5$value)
#> 'log Lik.' -286.9373 (df=4)
context_number(bin_multinom)
#> [1] 4
context_number(bin_multinom_5$value)
#> [1] 3

With three states or more, VGAM::vglm() also stops after mixvlmc.maxit iterations and reports convergence warnings, as shown below with the three-state time series:

elec_vglm <- covlmc(elec_dts, elec_cov, alpha = 0.1)
elec_vglm_5 <- withr::with_options(
  list(mixvlmc.maxit = 5),
  count_warnings(covlmc(elec_dts, elec_cov, alpha = 0.1))
)
elec_vglm_5$warnings
#> [1] 11
logLik(elec_vglm)
#> 'log Lik.' -487.0262 (df=13)
logLik(elec_vglm_5$value)
#> 'log Lik.' -487.2099 (df=13)

Here the context tree is the same (with 5 contexts), but the likelihood is slightly lower with at most 5 iterations, as some of the logistic models have not converged.

The default value of mixvlmc.maxit should be sufficient in most cases. It can be increased if stats::glm() or VGAM::vglm() report convergence warnings on contexts that are not separable. With nnet::multinom(), the absence of warning does not guarantee convergence: fitting the model again with a larger mixvlmc.maxit and comparing the results is the simplest check.

States and levels absent from a context

The data associated with a context do not necessarily contain all the states. In the example above, the low state is never followed by the high one, as shown by the detailed frequencies of the contexts:

contexts(model_glm, frequency = "detailed")
#>        context freq low typical high
#> 1          low  167 128      39    0
#> 2 low, typical   39  15      21    3
#> 3 typical,....  469  22     415   32
#> 4 high, ty....   45   2      32   11
#> 5         high  286   1      45  240

The states that never follow a context are ignored by the model of this context, which gives them a zero probability and has fewer coefficients: the model of the low context has only one row of coefficients (it describes the probability of typical relative to low) while the model of the high context has two. This holds for all the engines.

A practical consequence is that the likelihood of new data in which low is followed by high is zero. This is the case of the sixth week of the data set:

pc_week_6 <- powerconsumption[powerconsumption$week == 6, ]
elec_dts_6 <- cut(pc_week_6$active_power,
  breaks = c(0, 0.4, 2, 8),
  labels = c("low", "typical", "high")
)
elec_cov_6 <- data.frame(day = pc_week_6$hour >= 7 & pc_week_6$hour <= 17)
loglikelihood(model_glm, newdata = elec_dts_6, newcov = elec_cov_6)
#> 'log Lik.' -Inf (df= 13, nb obs.= 1006, initial="truncated")

Similarly, levels of factor covariates that are absent from the data of a context are ignored by its model. The engines report this differently: VGAM::vglm() gives no coefficient for those levels, while stats::glm() and nnet::multinom() give them a zero coefficient. We illustrate this with an artificial time series with three states whose dynamics depend on a factor covariate z with three levels. The level w can only be observed after state a:

set.seed(2)
nb_obs <- 600
probs <- list(u = c(0.6, 0.2, 0.2), v = c(0.2, 0.6, 0.2), w = c(0.2, 0.2, 0.6))
sim_x <- character(nb_obs)
sim_z <- character(nb_obs)
sim_x[1] <- "a"
sim_z[1] <- "w"
for (t in 2:nb_obs) {
  ## the next state depends on the previous value of the covariate
  sim_x[t] <- sample(c("a", "b", "c"), 1, prob = probs[[sim_z[t - 1]]])
  ## w is only observed after a
  if (sim_x[t] == "a") {
    sim_z[t] <- sample(c("u", "v", "w"), 1)
  } else {
    sim_z[t] <- sample(c("u", "v"), 1)
  }
}
sim_cov <- data.frame(z = factor(sim_z))
table(sim_x, sim_z)
#>      sim_z
#> sim_x   u   v   w
#>     a  81  78  78
#>     b 101 123   0
#>     c  71  68   0

In the contexts b and c, the level w is absent from the data. VGAM::vglm() reports no coefficient for it:

sim_glm <- covlmc(sim_x, sim_cov)
draw(sim_glm, model = "full")
#> ▪
#> ├─ a ([ (I)     • z_1v  z_1w  
#> │       -0.9676 • 1.59  0.5368
#> │       -1.427  • 1.044 2.238  ])
#> ├─ b ([ (I)     • z_1v  
#> │       -0.9163 • 1.67  
#> │       -1.261  • 0.8864 ])
#> └─ c ([ (I)    • z_1v 
#>         -1.006 • 2.392
#>         -1.006 • 1.173 ])

while nnet::multinom() reports a zero coefficient:

sim_multinom <- withr::with_options(
  list(mixvlmc.predictive = "multinom"),
  covlmc(sim_x, sim_cov)
)
draw(sim_multinom, model = "full")
#> ▪
#> ├─ a ([ (I)     • z_1v  z_1w  
#> │       -0.9676 • 1.59  0.5368
#> │       -1.427  • 1.044 2.238  ])
#> ├─ b ([ (I)     • z_1v   z_1w
#> │       -0.9163 • 1.67   0   
#> │       -1.261  • 0.8864 0    ])
#> └─ c ([ (I)    • z_1v  z_1w
#>         -1.006 • 2.392 0   
#>         -1.006 • 1.173 0    ])

In both cases, the coefficient of w in the contexts b and c is not estimated: the models are identical and so are their likelihoods.

logLik(sim_glm)
#> 'log Lik.' -574.9331 (df=14)
logLik(sim_multinom)
#> 'log Lik.' -574.9331 (df=14)

The LaTeX representation produced by draw() (see the article Drawing context trees and models) represents those coefficients by zeros whatever the engine, for instance with VGAM::vglm():

draw(sim_glm, "latex")
#> \begin{forest}
#> [\textbf{$\epsilon$}
#> [\multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{a}}\\\hline
#> {\small (I)}&{\small -0.9676}&{\small -1.427}\\
#> {\small $\text{z[v]}_{t-1}$}&{\small 1.59}&{\small 1.044}\\
#> {\small $\text{z[w]}_{t-1}$}&{\small 0.5368}&{\small 2.238}\\
#> , align=ccc]
#> [\multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{b}}\\\hline
#> {\small (I)}&{\small -0.9163}&{\small -1.261}\\
#> {\small $\text{z[v]}_{t-1}$}&{\small 1.67}&{\small 0.8864}\\
#> {\small $\text{z[w]}_{t-1}$}&{\small 0}&{\small 0}\\
#> , align=ccc]
#> [\multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{c}}\\\hline
#> {\small (I)}&{\small -1.006}&{\small -1.006}\\
#> {\small $\text{z[v]}_{t-1}$}&{\small 2.392}&{\small 1.173}\\
#> {\small $\text{z[w]}_{t-1}$}&{\small 0}&{\small 0}\\
#> , align=ccc]]
#> \end{forest}

Number of parameters

The number of parameters of a COVLMC, used by AIC() and BIC(), is the df attribute of its log likelihood (see the “Number of parameters” section of ?loglikelihood.covlmc). It does not depend on the engine: the coefficients that are not estimated, such as the ones of the states or levels absent from the data of a context, are not counted, regardless of the way the engine reports them.

More precisely, in a time series with \(s\) states, the model of a context followed by \(k\) different states in the data has \(s-1\) intercepts and \((k-1)p\) coefficients for the covariates, where \(p\) is the number of parameters associated with the covariates: for each time step of the memory of the model, one per numerical or logical covariate and the number of levels minus one per factor covariate (counting only the levels present in the data of the context). The \(s-1\) intercepts are counted even if some states never follow the context, as for the transition probabilities of a context of a VLMC: a context followed by a single state has therefore \(s-1\) parameters (see the next section). This ensures that each context has a cost in the information criteria, as in the theory of context tree selection. The following code recomputes the number of parameters of each context of the electricity consumption example from its detailed frequencies and from the memory of its model:

elec_ctx <- contexts(model_glm, frequency = "detailed", hsize = TRUE)
s <- length(states(model_glm))
k <- rowSums(elec_ctx[, as.character(states(model_glm))] > 0)
p <- elec_ctx$hsize
elec_ctx$parameters <- (s - 1) + (k - 1) * p
elec_ctx$nominal <- (s - 1) * (1 + p)
elec_ctx[, c("context", "hsize", "parameters", "nominal")]
#>        context hsize parameters nominal
#> 1          low     1          3       4
#> 2 low, typical     0          2       2
#> 3 typical,....     0          2       2
#> 4 high, ty....     0          2       2
#> 5         high     1          4       4
sum(elec_ctx$parameters)
#> [1] 13
attr(logLik(model_glm), "df")
#> [1] 13

For instance, the low context (first row) is followed by \(k = 2\) different states and its model has a memory of 1 time step of the logical covariate, thus \(p = 1\): its model has \(s-1 = 2\) intercepts and \((k-1)p = 1\) coefficient for the covariate, that is 3 parameters.

The likelihood ratio tests used by covlmc() to simplify the models use instead the nominal number of parameters, \((s-1)(1+p)\), where \(p\) counts all the levels of the factor covariates, as in the original algorithm. The two numbers differ only for the contexts whose model uses the covariates and that are not followed by all the states (such as the low context) or, with factor covariates, whose data do not contain all the levels. In this example, the sum of the nominal numbers of parameters of the contexts would be 14 instead of 13.

Degenerate contexts

When a context is always followed by the same state in the data, the maximum likelihood estimate of the probability of this state is one, and the logistic models are degenerate. covlmc() does not call the engine in this case but uses a constant model that does not depend on the covariates. Its probabilities are regularised: they are computed after adding pseudo_obs fake observations of each of the states to the observed ones. If the context is followed \(n\) times by the state \(x\) and the state space contains \(s\) states, the probability of \(x\) is \[ \frac{n+\text{pseudo\_obs}}{n+s\times\text{pseudo\_obs}}, \] while the other states have a probability of \(\frac{\text{pseudo\_obs}}{n+s\times\text{pseudo\_obs}}\). This corresponds to a Bayesian posterior mean estimation with a Dirichlet prior. The pseudo_obs parameter is set with covlmc_control() and defaults to 1.

We illustrate this with an artificial binary time series in which state 1 is always followed by state 0, while the probability of switching from 0 to 1 increases with a numerical covariate:

set.seed(1)
nb_obs <- 500
deg_cov <- data.frame(y = runif(nb_obs))
deg_x <- integer(nb_obs)
for (t in 2:nb_obs) {
  if (deg_x[t - 1] == 1) {
    deg_x[t] <- 0L
  } else {
    deg_x[t] <- rbinom(1, 1, 0.2 + 0.6 * deg_cov$y[t - 1])
  }
}
deg_model <- covlmc(deg_x, deg_cov)
draw(deg_model, model = "full")
#> ▪
#> ├─ 0 ([ (I)    • y_1  
#> │       -1.371 • 2.232 ])
#> └─ 1 ([ (I)  
#>         -5.03 ])

The context 1 has a constant model, with only an intercept. As the time series has two states, this intercept is the logit of the probability of state 1. In the data, the context is followed 152 times by state 0:

deg_ctx <- contexts(deg_model, frequency = "detailed", model = "coef")
deg_ctx
#>   context freq   0   1         coef
#> 1       0  347 195 152 -1.37084....
#> 2       1  152 152   0 -5.03043....

and the probability of state 1 after state 1 is therefore 1 / (n + 2) (with pseudo_obs = 1):

n_1 <- deg_ctx[["0"]][2]
plogis(deg_ctx$coef[[2]][1])
#> [1] 0.006493506
1 / (n_1 + 2)
#> [1] 0.006493506

The pseudo_obs parameter can be given to covlmc() (and to tune_covlmc()) via a control list created by covlmc_control(). covlmc() also accepts it directly as an argument, which is passed to covlmc_control(). Larger values lead to less extreme probabilities:

pseudo_obs_values <- c(0.1, 1, 10)
deg_models <- lapply(pseudo_obs_values, function(po) {
  covlmc(deg_x, deg_cov, control = covlmc_control(pseudo_obs = po))
})
data.frame(
  pseudo_obs = pseudo_obs_values,
  prob_1_after_1 = sapply(deg_models, function(m) {
    plogis(contexts(m, model = "coef")$coef[[2]][1])
  }),
  expected = pseudo_obs_values / (n_1 + 2 * pseudo_obs_values),
  loglikelihood = sapply(deg_models, function(m) as.numeric(logLik(m)))
)
#>   pseudo_obs prob_1_after_1     expected loglikelihood
#> 1        0.1   0.0006570302 0.0006570302     -222.8753
#> 2        1.0   0.0064935065 0.0064935065     -223.7656
#> 3       10.0   0.0581395349 0.0581395349     -231.8799

The regularised probabilities are used to compute the likelihood, which decreases when pseudo_obs increases as the probability of the observed transition decreases. Whatever the value of pseudo_obs, the model of a context followed by a single state has \(s-1\) parameters, its intercepts (see the previous section), so pseudo_obs has no effect on the number of parameters:

attr(logLik(deg_models[[1]]), "df")
#> [1] 3
attr(logLik(deg_models[[3]]), "df")
#> [1] 3

Notice that the regularisation applies only to contexts followed by a single state: in the other contexts, states that never follow the context have a zero probability, as explained above.

Memory occupation and trimming

What a COVLMC stores

A covlmc object contains the fitted engine objects (one per context, plus the ones used to compute the likelihood of the first observations, see vignette("likelihood")) as well as the data used to fit them. When keep_data = TRUE (the default value), covlmc() also stores the original time series and covariates, and caches some models, in order to enable post-pruning with prune() (and thus tune_covlmc()). The engine objects themselves store quantities whose size grows with the number of observations (such as fitted values and residuals) and their formulas reference the environment in which they were created.

As a consequence, COVLMC objects can be large. Two measures of size are given below: object.size() ignores environments, while the size of the serialised object includes them and corresponds to what is written by saveRDS() (without compression) or sent to the workers in parallel processing. Neither is exactly the memory used by the object in the R session.

obj_sizes <- function(...) {
  objects <- list(...)
  data.frame(
    object_size_kb = sapply(objects, function(o) {
      round(as.numeric(object.size(o)) / 1024)
    }),
    serialised_kb = sapply(objects, function(o) {
      round(length(serialize(o, NULL)) / 1024)
    })
  )
}
obj_sizes(
  "VGAM::vglm()" = model_glm,
  "nnet::multinom()" = model_multinom
)
#>                  object_size_kb serialised_kb
#> VGAM::vglm()               5264          2697
#> nnet::multinom()           1132           683

The two measures do not agree, as they do not account for the components of the objects in the same way, but both show that the models fitted by VGAM::vglm() are much larger than the ones fitted by nnet::multinom().

Trimming a model

The trim() function (see trim.covlmc()) removes the data and the cached models from a COVLMC. With keep_model = TRUE, the engine objects are kept but simplified (with butcher::butcher() for stats::glm() and nnet::multinom()) and the environments referenced by their formulas are discarded. With keep_model = FALSE (default), the engine objects are removed and only their coefficients are kept.

obj_sizes(
  "untrimmed" = model_glm,
  "trim(keep_model = TRUE)" = trim(model_glm, keep_model = TRUE),
  "trim()" = trim(model_glm)
)
#>                         object_size_kb serialised_kb
#> untrimmed                         5264          2697
#> trim(keep_model = TRUE)           3893           702
#> trim()                              36             7

The fully trimmed model is very small, but it supports fewer operations. The following table summarises what can be done with a model trimmed with keep_model = TRUE or keep_model = FALSE (see the documentation of the corresponding functions):

Operation TRUE FALSE
logLik(), AIC(), BIC() yes yes
draw(), contexts(model = "coef") yes yes
contexts(metrics = TRUE) yes yes
metrics() of the model (except the AUC) yes yes
contexts(model = "full") yes no
model(type = "full") yes no
loglikelihood() on new data yes no
predict(), simulate() yes no
positions(), contexts(positions = TRUE) no no
prune() no no

The metrics of a trimmed model are computed from the ones of its contexts (and of the first observations, computed by trim()): the accuracy and the confusion matrix are available, but the AUC is missing (with a warning). The likelihood of the original data is also preserved by trimming, while the likelihood of new data needs the engine objects:

elec_trimmed <- trim(model_glm)
logLik(elec_trimmed)
#> 'log Lik.' -487.0262 (df=13)
loglikelihood(trim(model_glm, keep_model = TRUE),
  newdata = elec_dts_6, newcov = elec_cov_6
)
#> 'log Lik.' -Inf (df= 13, nb obs.= 1006, initial="truncated")
loglikelihood(elec_trimmed, newdata = elec_dts_6, newcov = elec_cov_6)
#> Error in `loglikelihood.covlmc()`:
#> ! loglikelihood calculation for new data is not supported by fully trimmed covlmc

As prune() is not available for trimmed models, the trimming should be done once the model selection is completed.

Trimming in tune_covlmc()

tune_covlmc() builds a sequence of models by pruning an initial large model and can save some of them. The trimming argument specifies the trimming of the intermediate models ("full" by default, which corresponds to trim(), "partial", which corresponds to trim(keep_model = TRUE), or "none"), while best_trimming applies to the best model and to the initial one, which are not trimmed by default (see vignette("model-selection") and the “Memory occupation” section of ?tune_covlmc). Trimming all the models, including the best one, is recommended when memory is an issue, in particular when tune_covlmc() is called in parallel processing contexts:

elec_glm_trimmed <- tune_covlmc(elec_dts, elec_cov,
  criterion = "AIC",
  best_trimming = "full"
)
obj_sizes(
  "default" = elec_glm,
  "best_trimming = \"full\"" = elec_glm_trimmed
)
#>                        object_size_kb serialised_kb
#> default                          5267          2697
#> best_trimming = "full"             39             8

The trimmed result still gives access to the selected model and to the results of the selection process, for instance:

elec_glm_trimmed
#> VLMC with covariates context tree on low, typical, high 
#>  cutoff in quantile scale: 0.1715
#>  Number of contexts: 5 
#>  Maximum context length: 2 
#>  Selected by AIC (1000.052) with likelihood function "truncated" (-487.0262)
